title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 101 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
talk_summary: Laurie Voss (Arize) walks through a full eval loop for agents: instrument with OpenTelemetry tracing, read traces manually before writing evals, then build code evals, built-in LLM-judge evals, and custom rubrics, meta-evaluate the judge against human labels, and feed judge explanations back to a coding agent to rewrite prompts, verified by experiments on a fixed dataset. The core claim is that non-deterministic agents need a layered (Swiss-cheese) eval suite in CI to replace vibe-based shipping and to make model swaps and prompt changes measurable.

takeaways.technique: Feed judge explanations back to a coding agent as data-driven prompt fixes
takeaways.what_they_do: Export failing traces plus the LLM judge's natural-language explanations, hand the batch to a coding agent with the product requirements, and have it rewrite prompts; then re-run the same dataset as an experiment to prove the fix.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can take a whole bunch of explanations from a bunch of evals and pass them back to your coding agent
takeaways.numbers: Demo went from ~50% failing to 100% passing on a 12-example set (speaker notes this is unrealistically smooth)

takeaways.technique: Read traces before writing evals (open/axial coding)
takeaways.what_they_do: Manually read a dozen+ traces end to end, write free-form notes on each failure, then group into root-cause categories and rank by frequency x severity before writing any evaluator.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Read your traces before you write eval. Before you write a single evaluator start with your data.

takeaways.technique: Layered code evals + LLM-judge evals as merge gates
takeaways.what_they_do: Cheap deterministic checks (format, required strings, length) run first, then semantic LLM judges for correctness/faithfulness/actionability, each as a separate focused evaluator rather than one mega-evaluator.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you find yourself writing a rubric that lists six different things that the response should do, then stop. That is six evaluators, not one.

takeaways.technique: Meta-evaluate the judge against human labels; use a different lab's model as judge
takeaways.what_they_do: Label a golden set by hand, compare judge vs human agreement, compute precision/recall, and use a different model family for judging than for generation to avoid self-preference bias.
takeaways.evidence_quote: use both say OpenAI and Anthropic. Use one to do your agent and one to do the judging
takeaways.numbers: Human inter-rater reliability cited as low as 0.2-0.3; demo judge agreement 46% on random labels

takeaways.technique: Sample online evals instead of grading all traffic
takeaways.what_they_do: Run LLM-judge evals on a percentage of production traces (1-10%) rather than every run, and keep deterministic code evals on everything.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you sample 10% of your traffic or 1% of your traffic. Uh, and that gives you a directional signal

takeaways.technique: Fixed failure datasets + experiments for controlled comparison
takeaways.what_they_do: Save failing traces into a dataset, re-run the changed agent on the same inputs with the same evaluators so score deltas are attributable to the change; keep a separate passing set as regression.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you take the same inputs, the same evaluators and the only thing that changed is the agent's prompts
takeaways.numbers: 12-20 examples for directional signal; 200-400 for shipping decisions
